t: Number of Possible Sets of Closing Branches
o: With n ≤ 10 branches, enumerate all 2ⁿ subsets of closed branches; for each, run all-pairs shortest paths on the surviving nodes and verify every pair distance ≤ maxDistance. Example 2: 7 of 8 subsets survive. Floyd–Warshall per subset costs 2ⁿ·n³ ≈ 10⁶ operations — trivially fast.
k: n ≤ 10 makes bitmask enumeration the intended solution.
Floyd–Warshall restricted to active nodes; empty and single-node sets are automatically valid.

a.i: For each subset of open branches, initialize distances (0 on diagonal, road weights on edges, ∞ otherwise), run Floyd–Warshall over active intermediates, and count the subset if all active pairs are within maxDistance.
s: Build distance matrix from active roads
Count if all active pairs ≤ maxDistance

a.n: Approach 2: Precompute edge matrix, Dijkstra per subset
a.i: Same enumeration, but instead of Floyd per subset, run Dijkstra from each active source on the filtered graph — useful to showcase shortest-path tooling; slightly slower asymptotically but fine at this scale.

w: Bitmask + Floyd is the canonical answer here; mention that n ≤ 10 is the tell. Pitfalls: multiple roads between the same pair (take the min), remembering the empty set and single-node sets count as valid, and skipping inactive intermediate nodes in Floyd. Follow-up: what if n were 20? You'd need smarter pruning or meet-in-the-middle.
